author: west la times
title: Study finds shorter hormone therapy may suffice for many prostate cancer patients - West LA Times
text:
A new study led by researchers at the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center has found that most of the benefits from androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) for prostate cancer occur within the first 9 to 12 months of treatment. Extending ADT beyond this period provides only limited additional protection and increases the risk of health problems such as cardiovascular and metabolic issues.
The research, which analyzed data from over 10,000 men across 13 international clinical trials, suggests that the optimal duration of hormone therapy should be based on a patient’s specific cancer risk. The findings indicate that low-risk patients may not require ADT, intermediate-risk patients benefit most from six to twelve months of therapy, high-risk patients may benefit from up to twelve months, and very high-risk patients might need longer treatment.
Androgen deprivation therapy is often used with radiation to slow prostate cancer growth by lowering testosterone levels. While it is effective in controlling the disease, long-term use can lead to side effects like bone loss, muscle loss, and heart problems. Current guidelines recommend four to six months of ADT for intermediate-risk patients and up to three years for high-risk cases, but there has been uncertainty about how long treatment should last.
Dr. Amar Kishan, professor and executive vice chair of radiation oncology and co-director of the cancer molecular imaging, nanotechnology and theranostics program at UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center, commented on the importance of tailoring treatments: “Prostate cancer treatment should not be one-size-fits-all,” said Dr. Kishan. “These findings help doctors personalize therapy, balancing cancer control with potential side effects and other health risks.”
The study’s results underscore the value of creating personalized treatment plans for men with prostate cancer. By considering factors such as a patient’s overall health, age, preferences, and specific cancer risk level, physicians can reduce unnecessary exposure to hormone therapy while maintaining effective disease management.
The full study was published in JAMA Oncology. Other UCLA contributors include Luca Valle, Matthew Rettig, Tahmineh Romero and Michael Steinberg. The research received partial funding from grants provided by the National Institutes of Health.
